extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / scientists; readers of Newton's Principia (physicists, astronomers, philosophers of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the methodological rules and modelling assumptions Newton gives for doing experimental natural philosophy (his Regulae philosophandi and related modelling guidance). Intended for scientists reasoning from phenomena and building theoretical explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regula I (Parsimony / economy of causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Causas rerum naturalium non plures admitti dedere, quam quœ & veracœ sint & earum phœnomenis explicandis sufficiant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Philosophers say nature does nothing in vain, and that one should not multiply causes beyond what is true and sufficient to explain phenomena; prefer simpler accounts (nature is simple and does not luxuriate in superfluous causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regula II (Uniformity of causes for like effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideoque effectuum naturalium ejusdem generis eadem assignandœ sunt causœ, quatenus fieri potest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance / examples: Causes of natural effects of the same kind should, as far as possible, be assigned to the same sorts of causes (e.g., respiration in man and beast; a stone falling in Europe and America; light in a culinary fire and in the Sun; reflection of light on Earth and in the planets). Use analogy to extend causes across similar phenomena when justified by experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regula III (Generalize only from experiment — experimental universals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitates corporum quœ intendi & remitti nequeunt, quœque corporibus omnibus competent in quibus experimenta instituere hœc, pro qualitatibus corporum universorum habendœ sunt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Qualities of bodies are known only by experiment and so general qualities should be formulated only insofar as they agree with experiments; do not invent fanciful qualities contrary to experiment or by undue analogies. Sensible properties support universal claims only when they are common to all sensible cases. From observed properties (extension, hardness, impenetrability, mobility, vis inertiae) one may infer corresponding properties of component parts. Experimental evidence can justify broad inferences (e.g., universal gravitation) but avoid asserting untested properties for celestial bodies where experiment is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regula IV (Induction provisional — keep propositions from phenomena until contrary phenomena appear)
rubrics_metrics.description: In philosophia experimentali, propositiones ex phænomenis per inductionem collectæ, non obstantibus contrariis hypothesibus, pro veris aut accurate aut quâproximè haberi debent, donec alia occurrerint phænomena, per quœ aut accuratiores reddantur aut exceptionibus obnoxiœ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: In experimental philosophy, propositions collected by induction from phenomena should be regarded as true (or approximately true) despite contrary hypotheses, until further phenomena occur that make them more accurate or expose exceptions. This is to prevent hypotheses from undermining inductive arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modelling assumption for vortices (assume uniform fluidity/density unless evidence indicates otherwise)
rubrics_metrics.description: In his omnibus suppono fluidum ex materia quoad densitatem fluiditatem uniformi constare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance / elaboration: When investigating vortices Newton assumes a fluid of uniform density and fluidity. He notes how departures (regions of lower fluidity/greater thickness) alter behavior: less fluid regions cohere more, receive motion more slowly and propagate it less far; viscosity or reduced lubricity alters the predicted relation between period and distance. If the vessel is non-spherical, particle paths conform to vessel shape and periods relate approximately to squares of mean distances. These modelling assumptions should be stated and departures considered when comparing to observations.
